Our story

A river town, a Templar castle, and a very long way from where we started

We're bringing everyone we love to Tomar — the small town beneath the Convento de Cristo where the Knights Templar once made their home, cut through by the slow green Nabão river. It felt right for the same reason our life together has: something old, something built to last, somewhere worth the journey.

We'll say our vows at the Igreja de São João Baptista, Tomar's Manueline church on the main square, on 25 August 2027. From there, everyone's invited out to Casa da Avó Genoveva, among olive trees and stone walls, to eat, drink, dance, and probably not stop until very late.

This page has everything you need — where to stay, how to get here, and how to let us know you're coming. If anything's missing, just ask.

We wanted a wedding that felt like the town it's in — warm, unhurried, and a little bit timeless.

The town

A short history of Tomar

Tomar was founded in 1160 by Gualdim Pais, Grand Master of the Knights Templar, as a stronghold on the front line of the Reconquista — the centuries-long push to retake the Iberian Peninsula. The castle and the Convento de Cristo that crown the hill above town were built as much for defence as for devotion.

When the Templar order was dissolved across Europe in the 14th century, Portugal simply renamed it: the Order of Christ took its place, its wealth and its headquarters here in Tomar. A century later, that fortune helped fund the voyages of the Age of Discoveries — the Order's own cross was painted on the sails of Portuguese caravels, including, by tradition, those of Vasco da Gama.

What's left is one of Portugal's most extraordinary buildings: the Convento de Cristo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where five centuries of architecture — Romanesque, Gothic, Manueline, Renaissance — are stacked on top of each other around the Templars' round church. Below it, the old town is a quiet grid of cobbled streets, one of the best-preserved medieval Jewish quarters in Portugal, and a river you'll want an afternoon for.

While you're here

Convento de Cristo

The Templars' round church and its famous Manueline window, one of Portugal's most extraordinary buildings.

The Charola's paintings

Inside, the walls still carry 16th-century painted panels and gilding, added under King Manuel I.

Mouchão Park

A small island garden in the Nabão river, with a working 19th-century water wheel.

Sinagoga de Tomar

One of the few medieval synagogues left standing in Portugal, in the heart of the old Jewish quarter.

Fatias de Tomar

The town's own egg-yolk sweet — worth seeking out at least once.

Festa dos Tabuleiros

A centuries-old festival of flower-crowned bread trays, held every four years — ask us if the dates line up.

Igreja de Santa Maria do Olival

One of Tomar's oldest churches, just below the castle.

Its role in the Discoveries

The Templars' own mother church, and burial place of several Grand Masters — Portuguese navigators trained and worshipped here before setting out, which is why it's often called the mother church of the Age of Discoveries.

Aqueduto dos Pegões

A 16th-century aqueduct that once carried water down to the Convento de Cristo — nearly 6km of arches, some over 30 metres tall.

Who built it

Designed by the Italian military engineer Filippo Terzi and finished in 1614, it's considered one of the finest works of Renaissance engineering in Portugal.

Ermida de Nossa Senhora da Conceição

A small Renaissance chapel near the aqueduct, easy to miss and worth the detour.

A Renaissance gem

Attributed to the architect Diogo de Torralva, its austere, perfectly proportioned interior is considered one of the purest expressions of Renaissance architecture in Portugal.

Convento de Santa Iria

A riverside chapel dedicated to Tomar's patron saint, on the banks of the Nabão.

The legend behind it

Built in the 16th century on the spot where legend says Santa Iria was martyred, her body was said to have floated down the river to Santarém — a city named for her.

Quinta da Granja

A 16th-century estate just outside town, once a rest house for the friars of the Order of Christ.

A retreat for the friars

Donated to the Order of Christ in 1531, its manor house, chapel, dovecote and stone weir on the Nabão have been a protected heritage site since 1996.

Getting here

Travel & where to stay

The nearest airport is Lisbon (LIS), about 1 hour 40 minutes' drive from Tomar, or a similar journey by train to Tomar's own station. We'd suggest arriving on 24 August so you're rested for the day itself — most of us will be.

Good to know

Questions we expect you'll ask

What should I wear?+
Smart and celebratory. Late August in Tomar runs hot, and we'll be moving between a church and an outdoor terrace — light fabrics and comfortable shoes will serve you far better than heels sinking into a lawn.
How do we get from the church to the reception?+
It's a short drive — we're arranging shuttles between the two, details to follow. If you'd rather drive yourself, both venues have parking.
Are children welcome?+
Yes — we're delighted to have kids there, and there'll be plenty of family around to keep them company. Let us know ages when you RSVP so we can plan food and seating.
Can I bring a plus-one?+
If your invitation names a plus-one, they're very welcome — just include their name on the RSVP. If you're not sure, ask us directly.
Dietary requirements?+
There's a spot for that on the RSVP form below — tell us about allergies or preferences and we'll make sure the caterer knows.
Gifts?+
Your being there is genuinely enough. If you'd still like to give something, we're putting together a small honeymoon fund — details to follow closer to the date.
What's the weather like?+
Hot and dry — late August in central Portugal typically sits in the high 20s to mid-30s°C. Sun protection during the day, a light layer for after dark.
